newsitem.title: USA: Clinton assures Chile's Frei on free trade accord.
newsitem.headline: Clinton assures Chile's Frei on free trade accord.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton assured Chilean President Eduardo Frei on Wednesday he was committed to completing a free trade agreement with Chile and urged Congress to pass legislation to speed up the process.

"Our administration remains committed to concluding a comprehensive free trade agreement with Chile," Clinton said at a joint news conference with Frei, guest at the first state visit Clinton has held since he began his second term.

Clinton said he told Frei during Oval Office talks that he wanted to get so-called "fast track" trade negotiation authority from Congress. That would allow U.S. trade officials to negotiate an agreement with Chile without fear it would later be changed by Congress.
"I believe we must have fast track authority to conclude new trade agreements that open markets to America's products and that advance our values," Clinton said.
Chile was invited to join the North American Free Trade Agreement, which links the United States, Canada and Mexico, at the first Summit of the Americas in Miami in December 1994.

Chile has concluded agreements with Canada, Mexico and other Latin American countries and is negotiating a deal with the European Union. But the lack of fast track authority has delayed negotiations with the United States.
"The United States simply cannot afford to sit on the sidelines while others share in the fruits of Latin America's remarkable growth," Clinton said.
Clinton also said he had asked U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman to go to Chile to start a new consultative process on promoting farm trade between the two countries.
Chilean barriers to imports of U.S. poultry, beef, wheat and fruit were identified as key problems after a recent visit by House Agriculture Committee Chairman Bob Smith.

Frei, speaking through an interpreter, said bilateral trade with the United States had undergone an explosive increase and there were sensitive issues between the two countries, "especially in agricultural sectors."
Trade between the United States and Chile passed the $6 billion mark last year, with a $1.5 billion trade balance in favour of the United States.

At a welcoming ceremony on the White House South Lawn, Frei spoke of the need to promote freer trade among North and South America with an eye toward the second annual Summit of the Americas in Santiago in March 1998.
"What we need immediately is for our economies to flourish in full freedom, a freedom that allows us to produce and to trade as if there were no frontiers," Frei said.

The United States is one of the most important markets for Chilean salmon, wine and fresh fruit while U.S. companies are among the chief foreign investors in Chile with billions of dollars invested, mainly in mining.
On Capitol Hill, U.S. businesses worried about losing market share in Chile launched an effort to win congressional approval of fast track legislation.

As members of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce lobbied members of Congress, Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang told a House Ways and Means trade subcommittee that work on proposed fast track legislation was "well advanced" and that he hoped it could be delivered to Congress next month.
Frei, on a four-day visit to the United States, is to address a joint session of Congress on Thursday.
